content.title: About
content.content: Amaranth flour is a whole‑grain flour made from ground amaranth seeds. It has a nutty aroma, a mildly sweet taste, and a light‑brown color. The flour is gluten‑free, rich in protein, fiber, and micronutrients, making it popular in gluten‑free cooking.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Amaranth belongs to the Amaranthaceae family and was a staple food of ancient Andean and Mexican civilizations.
Amaranth seeds contain up to 16 % protein, higher than most cereals.
The flour retains most of the seed’s nutrients because it undergoes minimal processing.
Amaranth is often called a “pseudo‑cereal” because it is not a true grain but is used like one.
In Russia and CIS countries, amaranth flour is gaining popularity in diet and vegan nutrition.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Amaranth flour provides all essential amino acids, making it a valuable plant‑based protein source.

items.title: Gluten‑free
items.content: Suitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Rich in fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestive health and promotes satiety.

items.title: Packed with micronutrients
items.content: Contains iron, magnesium, calcium, zinc, and vitamin E, supporting metabolism and immunity.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Phytochemicals in amaranth help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to amaranth.

items.title: High oxalate content
items.content: Large amounts of oxalates can contribute to kidney stone formation in susceptible people.

items.title: Digestive reactions
items.content: Excessive intake may cause bloating and gas due to the high fiber content.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Amaranth flour can be used in baking (bread, cookies, muffins), for pancakes, as a coating for meat, or added to smoothies for extra nutrition. When substituting wheat flour, combine it with other gluten‑free flours (rice, buckwheat) in a 1:1 ratio to improve dough structure.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store amaranth flour in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For long‑term storage, keep it in the refrigerator or freezer to prevent fat oxidation.
